sources.title: Harvey Reall, Part III General Relativity, University of Cambridge lecture notes, 12 October 2022
sources.locator: Full 125-page PDF; §§8.6–8.7, printed pp. 108–110 (PDF pp. 109–111): metric volume integration, hypersurface flux, Stokes' theorem, and the non-null normal-flux formula.
sources.reading_extent: The complete relevant reasoning in §§8.6–8.7 was inspected in the full-text PDF. No claim is made that all 125 pages were read for this batch.

contents.name: Metric volume form and hypersurface integration in §§8.6–8.7

source_review.read_extent: Read the metric-volume integration and hypersurface pullback discussion in §§8.6–8.7, including its orientation convention.
source_review.supports: The use of the metric volume form and the current three-form pulled back to a hypersurface.
source_review.limitations: The local definition specifies its own C1 current, open-rectangle and finite coordinate-face conventions; the source is not used to replace those definitions.

contents.name: Stokes flux balance and the metric divergence theorem in §8.7

source_review.read_extent: Read the complete stated Stokes application and divergence-theorem reasoning in §8.7.
source_review.supports: The relationship between local divergence, integrated current production and boundary flux, including the side-flux term.
source_review.limitations: The source route uses smooth currents and non-null unit-normal faces. The owned theorem proves its C1 finite coordinate-box case directly and uses the current form on side faces.

contents.name: Unit-normal flux formula for a non-null hypersurface in §8.7

source_review.read_extent: Read the normal-flux formula and its induced-metric volume factor in §8.7.
source_review.supports: The geometric meaning of a hypersurface current flux as a normal component times induced volume.
source_review.limitations: The lemma proves the spacelike coordinate-slice identity directly by a Lorentzian block determinant and inverse calculation.

contents.name: Differential-form integration and Stokes theorem in §§2.4.4–2.4.5

source_review.read_extent: Read the definitions of form integration and the stated Stokes theorem in §§2.4.4–2.4.5.
source_review.supports: The form-based orientation and flux convention used to motivate the local current three-form.
source_review.limitations: The local coordinate definition fixes the full face orientation and coordinate formula explicitly.

contents.name: Curved-space divergence theorem and its non-null boundary restriction in §3.2.4

source_review.read_extent: Read the complete divergence-theorem statement and its boundary-type qualification in §3.2.4.
source_review.supports: The metric-density divergence convention and the limitation of a unit-normal boundary formula to non-null faces.
source_review.limitations: The finite rectangular proof uses coordinate FTC and the current-form face integral, so it also defines flux on null side faces.

contents.name: Finite charge change and zero-side-outflow condition in §4.5.5

source_review.read_extent: Read the full slice-charge and boundary-flux argument in §4.5.5, including its no-outflow condition for equal charges.
source_review.supports: The distinction between local conservation and conservation of charge inside a finite region with side exchange.
source_review.limitations: The local proof supplies the finite C1 rectangle calculation; no physical entropy premise or empirical conclusion is imported.

sources.locator: §10.5.1, Proposition 10.5.1: bounded sets are Jordan measurable exactly when their boundary has content zero.
sources.reading_extent: The complete relevant section and proposition proof were inspected.

contents.name: Boundary criterion for Jordan measurability, Proposition 10.5.1

source_review.read_extent: Read all of §10.5.1 and the proof of Proposition 10.5.1.
source_review.supports: The Jordan boundary criterion used to establish measurability of coordinate boxes and their endpoint variants.
source_review.limitations: The thin-slab covers and the integrability argument for mixed endpoint rectangles are proved locally.
